# Book I, Proposition 11

*A perpendicular from a point on a line*

> To draw a straight line at right angles to a given straight line from a given point on it.

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/11-idea.svg" alt="Mark off equal lengths either side of the point (red) and join their ends with equal lines to a peak (blue): the line from the peak down to the point stands at right angles (yellow)." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>Mark off equal lengths either side of the point (red) and join their ends with equal lines to a peak (blue): the line from the peak down to the point stands at right angles (yellow).</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/11.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.11, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

Let AB be the given straight line, and C the given point on it.

Thus it is required to draw from the point C a straight line at right angles to the straight line AB.

Let a point D be taken at random on AC;

let CE be made equal to CD; [I. 3]

on DE let the equilateral triangle FDE be constructed, [I. 1]

and let FC be joined;

I say that the straight line FC has been drawn at right angles to the given straight line AB from C the given point on it.

For, since DC is equal to CE,

and CF is common,

the two sides DC, CF are equal to the two sides EC, CF respectively;

and the base DF is equal to the base FE;

therefore the angle DCF is equal to the angle ECF; [I. 8]

and they are adjacent angles.

But, when a straight line set up on a straight line makes the adjacent angles equal to one another, each of the equal angles is right; [Def. 10]

therefore each of the angles DCF, FCE is right.

Therefore the straight line CF has been drawn at right angles to the given straight line AB from the given point C on it.

Q. E. F.

✅ Proved

From [`Elements/BookI/Prop11.lean`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop11.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments; the lines under each one are the Lean that carries it out.

```lean
/-! ## What Euclid reads off the figure -/

/-- Room to cut off `CE`. I.3 cuts a straight line off from a *greater* one, and
nothing says that `CB` is greater than `CD`; Postulate 2 produces a straight line
but says nothing of how far. So: with centre `C` and distance `CD` describe a
circle (Post. 3); the straight line `DC`, produced beyond the centre, cuts it
again at some `X` (System E, Intersections 5); and `CX` produced (Post. 2) is
greater than `CX`, that is, than `CD`. -/
theorem Prop11.produced {C D : Point} (hDC : D ≠ C) :
    ∃ G : Point, Between D C G ∧ ‖C D‖ < ‖C G‖ := by
  obtain ⟨L, hC, hD⟩ := Postulate1 C D hDC.symm
  obtain ⟨α, hCα, hDα⟩ := Postulate3 C D hDC.symm
  obtain ⟨X, hXα, -, hXCD⟩ := line_circle_beyond (centre_inside hCα) hC hD hDC
  obtain ⟨G, hCXG⟩ := produce (ne_of_between hXCD).symm
  refine ⟨G, between_of_between_right (between_symm hXCD) hCXG, ?_⟩
  rw [Definition15 hCα hDα hXα]
  exact len_lt_of_between hCXG

/-- The two halves of a straight line. If `C` lies between `D` and `E`, every
other point `P` of the straight line `DE` lies on the ray from `C` through `D` or
on the ray from `C` through `E`: either `C` is not between `P` and `D`, or it is,
and then it cannot also be between `P` and `E` (System E, Between 7). -/
theorem Prop11.either_ray {C D E P : Point} {L : Line} (hDCE : Between D C E)
    (hD : OnLine D L) (hC : OnLine C L) (hP : OnLine P L) (hPC : P ≠ C) :
    OnRay P C D ∨ OnRay P C E := by
  by_cases h : Between P C D
  · have hE : OnLine E L := on_line_of_between hDCE hD hC
    exact Or.inr ⟨(ne_of_between (between_symm hDCE)).symm, hPC, ⟨L, hC, hE, hP⟩,
      fun h' => not_between_of_between_between h h' hDCE⟩
  · exact Or.inl ⟨(ne_of_between hDCE).symm, hPC, ⟨L, hC, hD, hP⟩, h⟩

/-- To draw a straight line at right angles to a given straight line from a given point on it. -/
theorem Prop11 {A B C Q : Point} (hAB : A ≠ B) (hC : Collinear A B C) (hQ : ¬ Collinear A B Q) :
    ∃ F : Point, SameSideOf F Q A B ∧ ∀ P : Point, Collinear A B P → P ≠ C → ∠ P C F = ∟ := by
  -- Let AB be the given straight line, and C the given point on it.
  /- Lean needs the straight line AB by name (Post. 1), with C on it and Q off it. -/
  obtain ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB⟩ := Postulate1 A B hAB
  have on_AB : ∀ {P : Point}, Collinear A B P → OnLine P AB := by
    rintro P ⟨M, hA_M, hB_M, hP_M⟩
    rw [line_unique hAB hA_AB hB_AB hA_M hB_M]
    exact hP_M
  have hC_AB : OnLine C AB := on_AB hC
  have hQ_AB : ¬ OnLine Q AB := fun h => hQ ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB, h⟩
  -- Thus it is required to draw from the point C a straight line at right angles to the
  -- straight line AB.
  -- Let a point D be taken at random on AC;
  /- Euclid's figure has C between A and B. In Lean C may be any point of the
     straight line AB, even A itself, and then there is no AC to take D on: B
     will do. All the proof needs is a point D of AB other than C (System E,
     Points 3). -/
  obtain ⟨D, hD_AB, hDC⟩ : ∃ D : Point, OnLine D AB ∧ D ≠ C := by
    by_cases hCA : C = A
    · exact ⟨B, hB_AB, by rw [hCA]; exact hAB.symm⟩
    · obtain ⟨D, hD_AB, hADC, -⟩ := exists_point_between hA_AB hC_AB (Ne.symm hCA) []
      exact ⟨D, hD_AB, (ne_of_between (between_symm hADC)).symm⟩
  -- let CE be made equal to CD; [I. 3]
  /- CE is cut off from DC produced beyond C, far enough for I.3 to have a
     greater straight line to cut it from (`Prop11.produced`). So C lies between
     D and E: the figure's D, C, E in a row. -/
  obtain ⟨G, hDCG, hCD_CG⟩ := Prop11.produced hDC
  obtain ⟨E, hCEG, hCE_CD⟩ := Prop3 hDC.symm hCD_CG
  have hDCE : Between D C E := between_symm (between_inner (between_symm hCEG) (between_symm hDCG))
  have hE_AB : OnLine E AB := on_line_of_between hDCE hD_AB hC_AB
  have hDE : D ≠ E := ne_of_between_ends hDCE
  have hEC : E ≠ C := ne_of_between (between_symm hDCE)
  -- on DE let the equilateral triangle FDE be constructed, [I. 1]
  /- On Q's side of DE, which is Q's side of AB: one straight line passes
     through D and E. -/
  obtain ⟨F, ⟨-, hDE_EF, hEF_FD⟩, hFQ⟩ := Prop1 D E hDE Q
  have hF_Q : SameSide F Q AB :=
    (hFQ (Triangle.of_line hD_AB hE_AB hDE hQ_AB)).sameSide hD_AB hE_AB
  have hF_AB : ¬ OnLine F AB := not_on_line_of_same_side hF_Q
  -- and let FC be joined;
  have hFC : F ≠ C := fun h => hF_AB (h ▸ hC_AB)
  obtain ⟨FC, -, -⟩ := Postulate1 F C hFC
  -- I say that the straight line FC has been drawn at right angles to the given straight line
  -- AB from C the given point on it.
  -- For, since DC is equal to CE,
  have hDC_CE : ‖D C‖ = ‖C E‖ := (len_symm D C).trans hCE_CD.symm
  -- and CF is common,
  have hCF : ‖C F‖ = ‖C F‖ := rfl
  -- the two sides DC, CF are equal to the two sides EC, CF respectively;
  have hCD_CE : ‖C D‖ = ‖C E‖ := (len_symm C D).trans hDC_CE
  -- and the base DF is equal to the base FE;
  have hDF_EF : ‖D F‖ = ‖E F‖ := (len_symm D F).trans (hEF_FD.symm)
  -- therefore the angle DCF is equal to the angle ECF; [I. 8]
  have hCDF : Triangle C D F := Triangle.of_line hC_AB hD_AB hDC.symm hF_AB
  have hCEF : Triangle C E F := Triangle.of_line hC_AB hE_AB hEC.symm hF_AB
  have hDCF_ECF : ∠ D C F = ∠ E C F := Prop8 hCDF hCEF hCD_CE hCF hDF_EF
  -- and they are adjacent angles.
  /- Adjacent: C lies between D and E, and F is off the straight line DE. -/
  have hDCF_FCE : ∠ D C F = ∠ F C E := hDCF_ECF.trans (angle_symm hEC hFC)
  -- But, when a straight line set up on a straight line makes the adjacent angles equal to one
  -- another, each of the equal angles is right; [Def. 10]
  /- Definition 10 says what a right angle is, and Postulate 4 that every right
     angle is the right angle `∟`. -/
  have hDCF_right : IsRightAngle D C F := ⟨E, hDCE, hCDF.bac, hDCF_FCE⟩
  have hECF_right : IsRightAngle E C F :=
    ⟨D, between_symm hDCE, hCEF.bac, hDCF_ECF.symm.trans (angle_symm hDC hFC)⟩
  -- therefore each of the angles DCF, FCE is right.
  have hDCF : ∠ D C F = ∟ := Postulate4 hDCF_right
  have hFCE : ∠ F C E = ∟ := (angle_symm hFC hEC).trans (Postulate4 hECF_right)
  -- Therefore the straight line CF has been drawn at right angles to the given straight line
  -- AB from the given point C on it.
  /- Every other point P of AB lies on the ray from C through D, or on the ray
     from C through E (`Prop11.either_ray`), and the angle PCF is the angle DCF
     or the angle ECF (`angle_onRay_left` in Book Zero). -/
  refine ⟨F, SameSideOf.of_line hAB hA_AB hB_AB hF_Q, fun P hP hPC => ?_⟩
  rcases Prop11.either_ray hDCE hD_AB hC_AB (on_AB hP) hPC with hPD | hPE
  · rw [angle_onRay_left hPD hFC]
    exact hDCF
  · rw [angle_onRay_left hPE hFC, angle_symm hEC hFC]
    exact hFCE
  -- Q. E. F.
```

## Mishnah

**Room to cut off CE.** "Let CE be made equal to CD," says Euclid, citing I.3. Heath notes that the Greek verb, κείσθω, does duty for the passive of τίθημι, "to place", a word "constantly used in the sense of making, e.g., one straight line equal to another straight line" (vol. 1, p. 269). But I.3 cuts a less straight line off a greater one, and which greater? In the figure E falls on CB, yet nothing says CB is longer than CD, and C might even be B. Postulate 2 produces a straight line "continuously", but never says how far. So [`Prop11.produced`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop11.lean) makes room: a circle about C through D (Post. 3); the straight line DC, produced beyond the centre, cuts that circle again (System E, Intersections 5); and produced a little further still (Post. 2), it is greater than CD (Def. 15). I.3 cuts CE off it, and then C lies between D and E, which is what makes the angles at C adjacent. The circle has in fact already marked E, so Lean could do without I.3, but we cite it where Euclid does. The same step comes back in I.16, I.20, I.22 and I.24.

**A point at random on AC.** In Euclid's figure C lies between A and B, and D between A and C. In Lean C may be any point of the straight line AB, even A itself, and then there is no AC to take D on: B does instead. Otherwise D is taken between A and C (System E, Points 3). Nothing later cares where D is, so long as it is a point of AB other than C.

**On which side.** Euclid's FC could stand up on either side of AB. Our I.11 puts it on the side of a given point Q, because I.46 and I.48 will need the perpendicular on a particular side. I.1 builds its triangle on whichever side we name, so this costs one extra argument to I.1: the point Q, which is off DE because DE and AB are one straight line (System E, Generalities 1). Being on Q's side, F is off AB, so CDF and CEF really are the two triangles that I.8 compares (`Triangle.of_line`).

**Right, and the right angle.** Definition 10 says when an angle is right: when it is equal to the angle adjacent to it. In Lean, `IsRightAngle D C F` asks for a point on DC produced beyond C (here E) with the angle DCF equal to the angle FCE. The statement, though, speaks of `∟`, the one size that all right angles share, and it is Postulate 4, "that all right angles are equal to one another", that turns "right" into "equal to ∟". So Postulate 4 is on I.11's certificate, though Euclid cites only Def. 10.

**At right angles to the whole of AB.** Euclid proves two angles right, DCF and FCE, and concludes that CF is at right angles to AB. Our statement says it of every point P of AB other than C: the angle PCF is right. Two small facts bridge the gap. Every such P lies on the ray from C through D or on the ray from C through E ([`Prop11.either_ray`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop11.lean), from System E's Between 7: C can't lie both between P and D and between P and E, since it lies between D and E). And an angle doesn't change when an arm is traced through another point of the same ray (`angle_onRay_left` in Book Zero). Every rule cited is one of Avigad, Dean and Mumma's, read with LeanEuclid's careful Lean version open alongside; our thanks to them all.

**I.9 in disguise, and Apollonius.** De Morgan remarks that this proposition, which is "to bisect the angle made by a straight line and its continuation", should be a particular case of I.9, the constructions being the same. Heath: "This is certainly worth noting, though I doubt the advantage of rearranging the propositions in consequence" (vol. 1, pp. 269–270). In Lean the rearrangement isn't on offer: our I.9 asks for a triangle BAC, and a straight line with its continuation makes none. Apollonius, Proclus reports, drew the two circles of I.1 about D and E instead of citing it. Heath explains what Euclid gains: "This necessitates proving again that DF is equal to FE; whereas Euclid's assumption of the construction of I. 1 in the words 'let the equilateral triangle FDE be constructed' enables him to dispense with the drawing of circles and with the proof that DF is equal to FE at the same time" (vol. 1, p. 270). Lean agrees with Euclid: DF equal to FE is read straight off the statement of I.1. Heath adds, generously, that Apollonius' constructions "are entirely suitable for what we call practical geometry".

**Heron's perpendicular at the end.** Proclus also gives a construction for a perpendicular at the *end* of a straight line, "it being supposed (for the sake of argument) that we are not permitted to produce the straight line", and the commentary of an-Nairīzī attributes it to Heron (vol. 1, p. 270). Take any point C on AB, set up CE at right angles to AB as here, cut off CD equal to AC, bisect the angle ACE by CF (I.9), draw DF at right angles to CE, and join FA: by I.4 the angle at A equals the right angle at D.

**The modern way.** Put C at the origin and let u point along AB, so that D and E are −u and u. Then F is as far from one as from the other, |f + u|² = |f − u|², and that simplifies to f·u = 0: CF is perpendicular to AB. In the complex plane it is shorter still: multiplying by i turns AB through a right angle.
